    "Name": ["Amogh", "Othmane"],
    # very well (both)
    "Communication": [5, 5],
    # acceptable (both)
    "Data Analysis": [3, 3],
    # Othmane higher
    "Management": [3, 4],
    # doing well (both)
    "SQL": [4, 4],
    # Othmane higher; Amogh very close
    "Problem Solving": [4, 5],
    # doing well (both)
    "Leadership": [4, 4],
    # acceptable (both)
    "Computer Science": [3, 3],
    # Othmane doing well; Amogh slightly above
    "Operations": [5, 4],
    # Othmane doing well; Amogh close
    "Project Management": [3, 4],
    # doing well (both)
    "Business Process": [4, 4],
}

# Optional target levels for Business Analyst roles (1–5)
target_level = {
    "Communication": 5,
    "Data Analysis": 4,
    "Management": 4,
    "SQL": 4,
    "Problem Solving": 4,
    "Leadership": 4,
    "Computer Science": 3,
    "Operations": 4,
    "Project Management": 4,
    "Business Process": 4,
}

# -----------------------------
# 2) Build & validate dataframe
# -----------------------------
df_skills = pd.DataFrame(skills_data).set_index("Name")
df_skills = (
    df_skills.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
             .fillna(1).clip(1, 5).round().astype(int)
)

team_avg = df_skills.mean().rename("Team Avg (1–5)")
summary = pd.concat(
    [team_avg, df_skills.min().rename("Min"), df_skills.max().rename("Max")], axis=1
).sort_values("Team Avg (1–5)", ascending=False)

display(Markdown("### Team Skills — DataFrame (Updated)"))
display(df_skills)
display(Markdown("### Team Summary by Skill"))
display(summary)

# -----------------------------
# 3) Interactive heatmap
# -----------------------------
px.defaults.template = "plotly_white"
px.defaults.width = 980
px.defaults.height = 460

fig_heat = px.imshow(
    df_skills.values,
    x=df_skills.columns, y=df_skills.index,
    color_continuous_scale="Blues", zmin=1, zmax=5,
    labels=dict(color="Level (1–5)")
)
fig_heat.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="Skill Levels (1–5): Amogh & Othmane — Updated", x=0.02),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10),
    xaxis_title="Skill", yaxis_title="Member"
)
fig_heat.update_traces(hovertemplate="Member: %{y}<br>Skill: %{x}<br>Level: %{z}<extra></extra>")

# -----------------------------
# 4) Member comparison bars (dropdown to switch)
# -----------------------------
members = df_skills.index.tolist()
skills  = df_skills.columns.tolist()

def frame_for(member):
    d = pd.DataFrame({
        "Skill": skills,
        member: df_skills.loc[member, skills].values,
        "Team Avg": team_avg[skills].values
    }).sort_values(member, ascending=False)
    return [
        go.Bar(x=d[member], y=d["Skill"], orientation="h", name=member),
        go.Bar(x=d["Team Avg"], y=d["Skill"], orientation="h", name="Team Avg")
    ]

base = members[0]
fig_comp = go.Figure(data=frame_for(base))
fig_comp.update_layout(
    barmode="group",
    title=dict(text=f"Skill Profile — {base} vs Team Avg (Updated)", x=0.02),
    xaxis_title="Level (1–5)", yaxis_title="Skill",
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1)
)
fig_comp.frames = [go.Frame(name=m, data=frame_for(m)) for m in members]
fig_comp.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="dropdown", x=1.0, xanchor="right", y=1.15, yanchor="top",
        buttons=[dict(label=m, method="animate",
                      args=[[m], {"mode":"immediate","fromcurrent":True,
                                  "transition":{"duration":0},
                                  "frame":{"duration":0, "redraw":True}}]) for m in members]
    )]
)
fig_comp.show()

# -----------------------------
# 5) Radar: Team Avg vs Target (exec view)
# -----------------------------
target_series = pd.Series(target_level).reindex(skills).fillna(3).clip(1,5)
radar_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Skill": skills,
    "Team Avg": team_avg.reindex(skills).values,
    "Target": target_series.values
})
cats = radar_df["Skill"].tolist()
team_vals = radar_df["Team Avg"].tolist()
targ_vals = radar_df["Target"].tolist()
cats_closed = cats + [cats[0]]
team_closed = team_vals + [team_vals[0]]
targ_closed = targ_vals + [targ_vals[0]]

fig_radar = go.Figure()
fig_radar.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(r=team_closed, theta=cats_closed, fill='toself', name='Team Avg'))

gaps = (target_series - team_avg.reindex(skills)).sort_values(ascending=False)

           for s, g in top_gaps.items()]

# Compare Amogh & Othmane to industry requirements (focused skill list)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, re
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0) Team skill levels (1–5) based on your brief
# ------------------------------------------------------------
skills_data = {
    "Name": ["Amogh", "Othmane"],
    # communication: very well (both)
    "Communication": [5, 5],
    # data analysis: acceptable (both)
    "Data Analysis": [3, 3],
    # management: Othmane higher
    "Management": [3, 4],
    # SQL: doing well (both)
    "SQL": [4, 4],
    # problem solving: Othmane higher, Amogh very close
    "Problem Solving": [4, 5],
    # leadership: both doing well
    "Leadership": [4, 4],
    # computer science: acceptable (both)
    "Computer Science": [3, 3],
    # operations: Othmane doing well; Amogh slightly above
    "Operations": [5, 4],
    # project management: Othmane doing well; Amogh close
    "Project Management": [3, 4],
    # business process: both doing well
    "Business Process": [4, 4],
}
df_skills = pd.DataFrame(skills_data).set_index("Name")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Industry demand for the same skills (from Lightcast)
#    - tries cleaned file first, then raw
#    - parses skills columns and counts exact token matches
# ------------------------------------------------------------
def load_lightcast():
    for p in ["Data/lightcast_clean_final.csv", "Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv"]:
        try:
            return pd.read_csv(p, low_memory=False)
        except Exception:
            pass
    return None

jobs = load_lightcast()
selected_skills = list(df_skills.columns)

def market_counts_from_jobs(jobs_df, selected):
    if jobs_df is None:
        # fallback: equal weights if dataset not available
        return pd.DataFrame({"Skill": selected, "Mentions": [1]*len(selected)})

    skill_cols = [c for c in [
        "SKILLS_NAME","SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME","COMMON_SKILLS_NAME",
        "SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME","JOB_SKILLS","SKILL_NAME"
    ] if c in jobs_df.columns]
    if not skill_cols:
        return pd.DataFrame({"Skill": selected, "Mentions": [1]*len(selected)})

    # build a flat Series of atomic, lowercased skills
    tokens = []
    for c in skill_cols:
        s = (jobs_df[c].dropna().astype(str)
             .str.replace(r"\[|\]", "", regex=True)
             .str.replace('"', "", regex=False)
             .str.replace(r"\\n", " ", regex=True)
             .str.split(r"\s*,\s*|\|"))
        tokens.extend([t.strip().lower() for row in s for t in row if t and t.strip()])

    tok_series = pd.Series(tokens, dtype="string")
    counts = []
    for skill in selected:
        skill_l = skill.lower()
        counts.append(int((tok_series == skill_l).sum()))
    dfm = pd.DataFrame({"Skill": selected, "Mentions": counts})
    # if everything is zero (naming mismatch), give minimal nonzero so visuals still scale
    if dfm["Mentions"].sum() == 0:
        dfm["Mentions"] = 1
    return dfm

df_market = market_counts_from_jobs(jobs, selected_skills)

display(Markdown("### Industry Demand — Top Skills (Lightcast subset)"))
display(df_market.sort_values("Mentions", ascending=False))

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Team vs Market alignment table
#    Scale demand to 1–5 so it’s comparable to skill levels
# ------------------------------------------------------------
team_avg = df_skills.mean().rename("Team Avg (1–5)")
df_compare = df_market.merge(team_avg.rename_axis("Skill"), left_on="Skill", right_index=True, how="left")

# scale mentions → 1–5 (robust to constant series)
mmin, mmax = df_compare["Mentions"].min(), df_compare["Mentions"].max()
if mmax == mmin:
    df_compare["Scaled Demand (1–5)"] = 3
else:
    df_compare["Scaled Demand (1–5)"] = (1 + 4*(df_compare["Mentions"]-mmin)/(mmax-mmin)).round(2)

df_compare["Gap (Market - Team)"] = (df_compare["Scaled Demand (1–5)"] - df_compare["Team Avg (1–5)"]).round(2)

display(Markdown("### Team vs Market — Alignment"))
display(df_compare.sort_values("Gap (Market - Team)", ascending=False))

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Visualization 1 — Grouped bars (clean executive view)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
fig1 = go.Figure()
fig1.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=df_compare["Skill"], y=df_compare["Scaled Demand (1–5)"],
    name="Industry Demand (scaled)", marker_color="#1f77b4", opacity=0.70
))
fig1.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=df_compare["Skill"], y=df_compare["Team Avg (1–5)"],
    name="Team Average", marker_color="#ff7f0e", opacity=0.90
))
fig1.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="Market Demand vs Team Proficiency (1–5 scale)", x=0.02),
    barmode="group",
    xaxis_tickangle=-35,
    xaxis_title="Skill",
    yaxis_title="Level (1–5)",
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=120),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1)
)
fig1.show()

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Visualization 2 — Bubble chart (demand vs proficiency)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
fig2 = px.scatter(
    df_compare, x="Team Avg (1–5)", y="Scaled Demand (1–5)",
    size="Mentions", color="Gap (Market - Team)",
    hover_name="Skill", text="Skill",
    title="Skill Demand vs Team Proficiency — Gap View",
    color_continuous_scale="RdYlBu_r"
)
fig2.update_traces(
    textposition="top center",
    marker=dict(sizemode="area", line=dict(width=1, color="DarkSlateGrey"))
)
fig2.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Team Average (1–5)",
    yaxis_title="Market Demand (scaled 1–5)",
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10),
    height=600
)
fig2.show()

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) Top gaps (actionable list)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
top_gaps = df_compare.sort_values("Gap (Market - Team)", ascending=False).head(5)[
    ["Skill", "Team Avg (1–5)", "Scaled Demand (1–5)", "Gap (Market - Team)"]
]
display(Markdown("### 🔍 Top 5 Gaps to Prioritize"))
display(top_gaps)

# Quick narrative for BA audience
focus = ", ".join(top_gaps["Skill"].head(3).tolist())
display(Markdown(f"""
**Takeaway:** Team strengths show in **Communication, Leadership, SQL**, and **Business Process**.
Focus upskilling on: **{focus}** to align more tightly with market demand.  
Use short, portfolio-ready artifacts (dashboards, case studies, SQL challenge write-ups) to close gaps fast.
"""))

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# -------- LOAD --------

DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# -------- SALARY (annualized + outlier guard) --------

salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY"), errors="coerce")
pp_col = df.get("ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD")
is_annual = (pp_col.astype(str).str.lower().str.strip().isin(["year","annual","annually","yr"])) if (pp_col is not None) else pd.Series(True, index=df.index)
salary_main = salary_main.where(is_annual, np.nan)

salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_FROM"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_TO"),   errors="coerce")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary_alt  = salary_alt.where(is_annual, np.nan)
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)

# Trim extreme outliers if we have enough non-null salary

q_ok = salary.notna().sum() > 200
q_lo, q_hi = (salary.quantile(0.05), salary.quantile(0.995)) if q_ok else (None, None)
salary = salary.mask(q_ok & ((salary < q_lo) | (salary > q_hi)))

# -------- EXPERIENCE --------

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max).fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)
experience = experience.mask(experience < 0)

# -------- REMOTE FLAG --------

remote = df.get("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").astype(str).str.lower().isin(
["remote","hybrid","remote/hybrid","remote - usa","remote - us"]
).astype("int8")

# -------- STATE (top 10 one-hot) --------

state = df.get("STATE_NAME").astype(str)
top_states = state.value_counts().nlargest(10).index
state_10 = state.where(state.isin(top_states), "OTHER")
state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(state_10, prefix="state", dtype="int8")

# -------- SKILLS (BoW top-50) --------

skills_text = (
df.get("SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("COMMON_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str)
)

# keep '-' escaped in regex class

vec = CountVectorizer(lowercase=True, token_pattern=r"[A-Za-z][A-Za-z+-.#]{1,}", max_features=50)
skills_bow = pd.DataFrame(vec.fit_transform(skills_text).toarray(),
columns=[f"kw_{t}" for t in vec.get_feature_names_out()])

# -------- FEATURE MATRIX --------

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"salary": salary, "experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies,
skills_bow
], axis=1)

valid = X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X[valid].fillna(0).astype(float)

rows_total = len(df); rows_used = len(X)
sal_nonnull = int(X["salary"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "salary" in X.columns else 0
exp_nonnull = int(X["experience"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "experience" in X.columns else 0
display(Markdown(f"- **Feature matrix:** {rows_used:,} rows × {X.shape[1]} features  (coverage — salary: {sal_nonnull:,}, experience: {exp_nonnull:,})"))

# Optional sample for speed (increase/remove if needed)

MAX_ROWS = 20000
Xs = X.sample(n=MAX_ROWS, random_state=42) if len(X) > MAX_ROWS else X

# -------- SCALE --------

scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(Xs)

# -------- CHOOSE K (loop-free) --------

Ks = list(range(3, 8))
fits    = [KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled) for k in Ks]
inertia = [m.inertia_ for m in fits]
sil     = [silhouette_score(Xs_scaled, m.labels_) for m in fits]
best_k  = Ks[int(np.argmax(sil))]
display(Markdown(f"**Chosen K:** {best_k} (max silhouette)"))

# -------- INTERACTIVE PLOTS --------

fig_elbow = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=inertia, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_elbow.update_layout(title="Elbow Curve (Inertia) vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Inertia",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_elbow.show()

fig_sil = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=sil, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_sil.update_layout(title="Silhouette Score vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Silhouette",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_sil.show()

# -------- FINAL K-MEANS --------

km = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled)
clusters = pd.Series(km.labels_, index=Xs.index, name="cluster")

# Scatter: salary vs experience (interactive)

df_scatter = pd.DataFrame({"salary": Xs.get("salary"), "experience": Xs.get("experience"), "cluster": clusters.astype(str)}).dropna()
(len(df_scatter) > 0) and px.scatter(
df_scatter, x="salary", y="experience", color="cluster",
title="K-Means Clusters — Salary vs Experience (sample)",
hover_data={"salary":":,.0f","experience":":.1f","cluster":True}
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

# Centers back-transformed (first 3 numeric features if present)

cent_cols = [c for c in ["salary","experience","remote"] if c in Xs.columns]
cent_idx  = [Xs.columns.get_loc(c) for c in cent_cols]
cent_full = km.cluster_centers_

# pad centers to Xs width before inverse_transform (no loops, pad with zeros)

pad_w = Xs.shape[1] - cent_full.shape[1]
cent_inv = scaler.inverse_transform(np.hstack([cent_full, np.zeros((cent_full.shape[0], pad_w))]))[:, cent_idx]
centers_df = pd.DataFrame(cent_inv, columns=[f"{c}~center" for c in cent_cols])
display(Markdown("### Cluster Centers (approx; numeric features)")); display(centers_df.round(2))

# -------- REFERENCE LABEL CROSSTABS (SOC/NAICS/ONET) --------

idx = Xs.index
ct_soc2  = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "SOC_2_NAME"])        if "SOC_2_NAME"        in df.columns else None)
ct_naics = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "NAICS_2022_2_NAME"]) if "NAICS_2022_2_NAME" in df.columns else None)
ct_onet  = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "ONET_NAME"])         if "ONET_NAME"         in df.columns else None)

(ct_soc2  is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × SOC_2_NAME (top categories)"))  and display(ct_soc2.loc[:,  ct_soc2.sum().nlargest(8).index])
(ct_naics is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × NAICS_2022_2_NAME (top categories)")) and display(ct_naics.loc[:, ct_naics.sum().nlargest(8).index])
(ct_onet  is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × ONET_NAME (top categories)"))   and display(ct_onet.loc[:,  ct_onet.sum().nlargest(8).index])

# Optional stacked bar for SOC_2_NAME

(ct_soc2 is not None) and px.bar(
ct_soc2.loc[:, ct_soc2.sum().nlargest(8).index].T, barmode="stack",
title="SOC (Top) Composition by Cluster",
labels={"value":"Count","variable":"Cluster","index":"SOC Category"}
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

# ---------- LOAD ----------

DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# ---------- SALARY (flat logic, no indents) ----------

salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY"), errors="coerce")
pay_period = df.get("ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD")

pp = pay_period.astype(str).str.lower().str.strip() if pay_period is not None else pd.Series("year", index=df.index)
is_annual = pp.isin(["year", "annual", "annually", "yr"])
salary_main = salary_main.where(is_annual, np.nan)

salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_FROM"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_TO"),   errors="coerce")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary_alt  = salary_alt.where(is_annual, np.nan)
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)
salary      = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))  # trim outliers

# ---------- FEATURES ----------

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max)
experience = experience.fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)

remote = df.get("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").astype(str).str.lower().isin(
["remote", "hybrid", "remote/hybrid", "remote - usa", "remote - us"]
).astype("int8")

state = df.get("STATE_NAME").astype(str)
top_states = state.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
state_8 = state.where(state.isin(top_states), "OTHER")
state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(state_8, prefix="state", dtype="int8")

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies
], axis=1)

# Keep only rows with valid salary

valid = salary.notna() & X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X.loc[valid].fillna(0)
y = salary.loc[valid]

display(Markdown(f"- **Training set size:** {len(X):,} rows, {X.shape[1]} features"))

# ---------- TRAIN/TEST SPLIT ----------

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# ---------- SCALE NUMERIC ----------

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# ---------- MODEL A: Linear Regression ----------

linreg = LinearRegression()

rmse_lr = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_lr))

display(Markdown(f"### Multiple Linear Regression Results"))
display(Markdown(f"**R²:** {r2_lr:.3f}  **RMSE:** ${rmse_lr:,.0f}"))

)

))

# Feature Importance

importances = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True)

})

# -------- SKILLS (BoW top-50) --------

df.get("SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("COMMON_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str)
)

# keep '-' escaped in regex class

vec = CountVectorizer(lowercase=True, token_pattern=r"[A-Za-z][A-Za-z+-.#]{1,}", max_features=50)
skills_bow = pd.DataFrame(vec.fit_transform(skills_text).toarray(),
columns=[f"kw_{t}" for t in vec.get_feature_names_out()])

# -------- FEATURE MATRIX --------

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"salary": salary, "experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies,
skills_bow
], axis=1)

valid = X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X[valid].fillna(0).astype(float)

rows_total = len(df); rows_used = len(X)
sal_nonnull = int(X["salary"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "salary" in X.columns else 0
exp_nonnull = int(X["experience"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "experience" in X.columns else 0
display(Markdown(f"- **Feature matrix:** {rows_used:,} rows × {X.shape[1]} features  (coverage — salary: {sal_nonnull:,}, experience: {exp_nonnull:,})"))

# Optional sample for speed (increase/remove if needed)

MAX_ROWS = 20000
Xs = X.sample(n=MAX_ROWS, random_state=42) if len(X) > MAX_ROWS else X

# -------- SCALE --------

scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(Xs)

# -------- CHOOSE K (loop-free) --------

Ks = list(range(3, 8))
fits    = [KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled) for k in Ks]
inertia = [m.inertia_ for m in fits]
sil     = [silhouette_score(Xs_scaled, m.labels_) for m in fits]
best_k  = Ks[int(np.argmax(sil))]
display(Markdown(f"**Chosen K:** {best_k} (max silhouette)"))

# -------- INTERACTIVE PLOTS --------

fig_elbow = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=inertia, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_elbow.update_layout(title="Elbow Curve (Inertia) vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Inertia",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_elbow.show()

fig_sil = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=sil, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_sil.update_layout(title="Silhouette Score vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Silhouette",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_sil.show()

# -------- FINAL K-MEANS --------

km = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled)
clusters = pd.Series(km.labels_, index=Xs.index, name="cluster")

# Scatter: salary vs experience (interactive)

df_scatter = pd.DataFrame({"salary": Xs.get("salary"), "experience": Xs.get("experience"), "cluster": clusters.astype(str)}).dropna()
(len(df_scatter) > 0) and px.scatter(
df_scatter, x="salary", y="experience", color="cluster",
title="K-Means Clusters — Salary vs Experience (sample)",
hover_data={"salary":":,.0f","experience":":.1f","cluster":True}
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

# Centers back-transformed (first 3 numeric features if present)

cent_cols = [c for c in ["salary","experience","remote"] if c in Xs.columns]
cent_idx  = [Xs.columns.get_loc(c) for c in cent_cols]
cent_full = km.cluster_centers_

# pad centers to Xs width before inverse_transform (no loops, pad with zeros)

pad_w = Xs.shape[1] - cent_full.shape[1]
cent_inv = scaler.inverse_transform(np.hstack([cent_full, np.zeros((cent_full.shape[0], pad_w))]))[:, cent_idx]
centers_df = pd.DataFrame(cent_inv, columns=[f"{c}~center" for c in cent_cols])
display(Markdown("### Cluster Centers (approx; numeric features)")); display(centers_df.round(2))

# -------- REFERENCE LABEL CROSSTABS (SOC/NAICS/ONET) --------

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_squared_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# ---------- LOAD ----------

DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# ---------- SALARY (flat logic, no indents) ----------

salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY"), errors="coerce")
pay_period = df.get("ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD")

pp = pay_period.astype(str).str.lower().str.strip() if pay_period is not None else pd.Series("year", index=df.index)
is_annual = pp.isin(["year", "annual", "annually", "yr"])
salary_main = salary_main.where(is_annual, np.nan)

salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_FROM"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_TO"),   errors="coerce")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary_alt  = salary_alt.where(is_annual, np.nan)
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)
salary      = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))  # trim outliers

# ---------- FEATURES ----------

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max)
experience = experience.fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)

remote = df.get("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").astype(str).str.lower().isin(
["remote", "hybrid", "remote/hybrid", "remote - usa", "remote - us"]
).astype("int8")

state = df.get("STATE_NAME").astype(str)
top_states = state.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
state_8 = state.where(state.isin(top_states), "OTHER")
state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(state_8, prefix="state", dtype="int8")

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies
], axis=1)

# Keep only rows with valid salary

valid = salary.notna() & X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X.loc[valid].fillna(0)
y = salary.loc[valid]

display(Markdown(f"- **Training set size:** {len(X):,} rows, {X.shape[1]} features"))

# ---------- TRAIN/TEST SPLIT ----------

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# ---------- SCALE NUMERIC ----------

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# ---------- MODEL A: Linear Regression ----------

linreg = LinearRegression()
linreg.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred_lr = linreg.predict(X_test_scaled)

r2_lr = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_lr)
rmse_lr = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_lr))

display(Markdown(f"### Multiple Linear Regression Results"))
display(Markdown(f"**R²:** {r2_lr:.3f}  **RMSE:** ${rmse_lr:,.0f}"))

# Scatter: Actual vs Predicted

fig_lr = px.scatter(
x=y_test, y=y_pred_lr,
labels={"x":"Actual Salary","y":"Predicted Salary"},
title="Linear Regression — Actual vs Predicted Salary"
)
fig_lr.add_trace(go.Scatter(
x=[y.min(), y.max()], y=[y.min(), y.max()],
mode="lines", name="Ideal", line=dict(color="red", dash="dot")
))
fig_lr.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10))
fig_lr.show()

# ---------- MODEL B: Random Forest ----------

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=120, random_state=42, max_depth=10, n_jobs=-1)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_test)

r2_rf = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_rf)
rmse_rf = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_rf))

display(Markdown(f"### Random Forest Regression Results"))
display(Markdown(f"**R²:** {r2_rf:.3f}  **RMSE:** ${rmse_rf:,.0f}"))

# Feature Importance

importances = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True)
fig_imp = px.bar(
importances, orientation="h",
title="Random Forest Feature Importance",
labels={"value":"Importance","index":"Feature"}
)
fig_imp.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10))
fig_imp.show()

# ---------- COMPARISON ----------

results_df = pd.DataFrame({
"Model": ["Linear Regression", "Random Forest"],
"R²": [r2_lr, r2_rf],
"RMSE": [rmse_lr, rmse_rf]
})
display(Markdown("### Model Comparison Summary"))
display(results_df.round(3))

title: AI vs. Non-AI Careers: Job Market Prospects in 2024
text:
Introduction
As of 2024, the global job market stands at a crucial crossroads, significantly shaped by the ongoing evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). This technology is transforming various sectors, including healthcare, finance, retail, and education. The shifts aren’t just about the types of jobs available; they’re also changing the way we work. Current studies reveal that while AI drives job displacement in routine and clerical roles, it simultaneously creates new opportunities that focus on technology, data, and human interaction (George ((2024)); Huang ((2024))). Tools like ChatGPT have added complexity, with predictions suggesting that over 30% of jobs could experience significant changes (Zarifhonarvar ((2024))). New roles, such as AI Solutions Architect and AI Bias Auditor, are emerging, highlighting the need for expertise in integrating AI into our workflows (George and George ((2025))). It’s clear that AI is not just about taking jobs away; it’s also sparking transformation, urging us to adapt, keep learning, and embrace innovation as we navigate the evolving career landscape.
As AI has gone from murmurs in the background to its sudden immediate dependencies for many many things in today’s age, questions, typically from fear, arise in the eye of the public. Will AI get rid of many jobs, crippling the job market? How is my job security in my current role going to change over the next couple of years? While AI brings humanity many benefits, it also has a very large grey area that could shift society in a negative direction if not managed properly. One thing that always pushes people forward in times of immense and sudden change, such as now, is to adapt. Rion ((2025)) states that “…there is a reduced risk of displacement occurring for high-skilled workers with AI encompassing elements of enhancement, whereas low-skilled workers are most at risk of displacement” (p. 2). The big hope with AI is that job displacement could potentially evolve into certain jobs and industries being repurposed for AI-centric functionalities. The change that AI has brought to the world and will continuously do, and in even bigger waves, is quickly making businesses adapt to the immediate benefits that it brings, but this is also a signal that individuals must pick up these skills to have a fighting chance in a job market that is turning into something entirely different.


Research Rationale
The increasing involvement of AI in various industries necessitates a deeper understanding of its impact on employment. Many conversations often frame AI as a threat to job security, but the reality is more nuanced. Research indicates that AI often triggers changes in work dynamics instead of leading to outright job loss. While there is no denial that some occupations in a number of sectors will be significantly altered if not replaced, as George ((2024)) points out, “AI is expected to result in more job movement than job elimination by boosting productivity, driving economic growth, altering job structures, and enabling sectors to transition” (p. 17). Recognizing these trends is crucial for both workers and policymakers as they work on strategies to ensure smooth transitions and equitable opportunities.
Additionally, the speed of this transformation is unlike anything we’ve seen before. Historical technological shifts unfolded over decades, while AI adoption is rapidly changing industries in just a few years. Today, workers find themselves in a labor market where traditional career paths exist alongside new, AI-driven opportunities. Zarifhonarvar ((2024)) emphasizes this urgency by stating, “32.8% of occupations could be fully impacted by ChatGPT, while 36.5% might experience a partial impact and 30.7% are likely to remain unaffected” (p. 100). This highlights the extensive and uneven impacts of AI disruption, emphasizing the need to examine its implications for job security, industry demand, and the emergence of new career fields. The function of this study is to assess the current state of the impact of AI on society, as of 2024, and try to get a better understanding of its pros and cons on the job market. According to Shen ((2024)), “AI technology is correlated with increasing the total number of jobs on the market. Thanks to more efficient labor productivity, capital deepening, and specialized division of labor from integrating digital technology, AI offsets the negative effects of robots on employment and significantly increases manufacturing enterprises’ market size and production scale, with a significant job creation effect” (p. 1). With the increased rate of integration of AI in most processes nowadays, there is actually a shift in the market and less of a depletion of jobs/job growth. Low-skilled workers have the biggest risk of being replaced by AI simply because the most mundane, repeatable jobs are the easiest for machines to replace. Developing certain skills relating to AI will prove very useful in this current job market because it is still such a fresh concept to the general population.


Literature Review
Recent research suggests that AI is more likely to lead to job shifting rather than large-scale, permanent job losses. While it’s true that some sectors may experience job displacement, George ((2024)) argues that the productivity gains associated with AI adoption consistently generate new employment opportunities. He explains that “displaced workers can transfer into new occupational jobs with adequate skilling and transition support rather than facing long periods of unemployment” (p. 17). This theme aligns with broader economic evidence showing that technological advancements typically create more jobs than they eliminate, even if the transition process can be rocky.
New job categories are emerging that didn’t exist just a decade ago. George and George ((2025)) highlight roles such as AI Solutions Architect and AI Bias Auditor, stating they are “not optional additions but essential components of sustainable AI strategy” (p. 58). Huang ((2024)) also notes that AI adoption is reshaping labor and capital in various industries, creating fresh opportunities while widening existing skill gaps. These trends underscore that AI isn’t merely automating routine tasks; it’s also driving innovation in job design, making continuous adaptation and skill development essential for today’s workforce.


Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with visualizations.
The Lightcast CSV file has a tremendous amount of data that would not make much sense to sort through manually. As a result, we have developed multiple tables that show a sample of the data from the Lightcast CSV. We show a sample of the first five rows which are raw and uncleaned. The second table is essentially a visualizer for the user showing how many rows, columns, and total missing cells there are in the file. The third table serves as a hub of information showing the percentage of data missing from the top 12 columns with the most missing data along with their types. The fourth table shows the data from the first table, but in a much cleaner fashion with all the relevant columns. The fifth tables is a comparative visual of how much data we were able to clean and filter throughout the entire process. As you can see, there are significantly less rows, columns, and total missing cells than before the cleanup. In the sixth and final table, all of the columns that had a certain percentage of missing data now have a missing data percentage of zero. This further shows that our process of cleaning up and filtering the data to pinpoint the exact information needed was successful.







References

George, Dr. A. S., and A. S. H. George. (2025): “The AI job revolution - how emerging roles are reshaping the future of work and creating new career pathways,” Zenodo, 3, 58–61.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import warnings
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display

# Suppress warnings (like DtypeWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# Load dataset
csv_path  = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, low_memory=False)

# Helper function for missing value summary
def missing_summary(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    ms = frame.isna().mean().mul(100).round(1).rename("% missing")
    dt = frame.dtypes.astype(str).rename("dtype")
    return pd.concat([dt, ms], axis=1).sort_values("% missing", ascending=False)

# Baseline snapshot (before cleaning)
rows_before, cols_before = df.shape
missing_cells_before = int(df.isna().sum().sum())
baseline_overview = pd.DataFrame({
    "metric": ["rows","columns","total missing cells"],
    "before": [rows_before, cols_before, missing_cells_before]
})
baseline_top_missing = missing_summary(df).head(12)

# Show initial outputs
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 1: Preview of raw dataset (first 5 rows)": []}))
display(df.head())
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 2: Baseline dataset overview": []}))
display(baseline_overview)
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 3: Top 12 most-missing columns (before cleaning)": []}))
display(baseline_top_missing)

# ============================
# Cleaning & Conversions
# ============================

# Standardize column names
df.columns = (df.columns.str.strip()
              .str.replace(r"\s+", "_", regex=True)
              .str.upper())

# Drop irrelevant columns
to_drop = ["ID","URL","ACTIVE_URLS","DUPLICATES","LAST_UPDATED_TIMESTAMP",
           "NAICS2","NAICS3","NAICS4","NAICS5","NAICS6","SOC_2","SOC_3","SOC_5"]
df.drop(columns=[c for c in to_drop if c in df.columns],
        inplace=True, errors="ignore")

# Convert dates
for col in [c for c in ["POSTED","UPDATED","DATE","JOB_POST_DATE"] if c in df.columns]:
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], errors="coerce")

# Convert salary columns
for col in ["SALARY","MINSALARY","MAXSALARY","ANNUAL_SALARY","HOURLY_RATE","PAY"]:
    if col in df.columns:
        df[col] = (df[col].astype(str)
                   .str.replace(r"[^0-9.\-]", "", regex=True)
                   .replace({"": np.nan, "-": np.nan})
                   .astype(float))

# Drop columns with >50% missing
df.dropna(axis=1, thresh=int(len(df)*0.5), inplace=True)

# Fill missing numeric values
num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()
if num_cols:
    if "INDUSTRY" in df.columns:
        df[num_cols] = df[num_cols].fillna(df.groupby("INDUSTRY")[num_cols].transform("median"))
    df[num_cols] = df[num_cols].fillna(df[num_cols].median())

# Fill missing categoricals with "Unknown"
for c in df.select_dtypes(include=["object"]).columns:
    df[c] = df[c].fillna("Unknown")

# Remove duplicates by key fields
dup_key = [c for c in ["TITLE","COMPANY","LOCATION","POSTED"] if c in df.columns]
if dup_key:
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=dup_key, keep="first")

# Snapshot after cleaning
rows_after, cols_after = df.shape
missing_cells_after = int(df.isna().sum().sum())
summary_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "metric": ["rows","columns","total missing cells"],
    "before": [rows_before, cols_before, missing_cells_before],
    "after":  [rows_after,  cols_after,  missing_cells_after]
})
after_top_missing = missing_summary(df).head(12)

# Show cleaned outputs
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 4: Cleaned dataset preview (first 5 rows)": []}))
display(df.head())

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import warnings
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display

# Suppress warnings (like DtypeWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# Load dataset
csv_path  = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, low_memory=False)

# Helper function for missing value summary
def missing_summary(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    ms = frame.isna().mean().mul(100).round(1).rename("% missing")
    dt = frame.dtypes.astype(str).rename("dtype")
    return pd.concat([dt, ms], axis=1).sort_values("% missing", ascending=False)

# Baseline snapshot (before cleaning)
rows_before, cols_before = df.shape
missing_cells_before = int(df.isna().sum().sum())
baseline_overview = pd.DataFrame({
    "metric": ["rows","columns","total missing cells"],
    "before": [rows_before, cols_before, missing_cells_before]
})
baseline_top_missing = missing_summary(df).head(12)

# Show initial outputs
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 1: Preview of raw dataset (first 5 rows)": []}))
display(df.head())
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 2: Baseline dataset overview": []}))
display(baseline_overview)
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 3: Top 12 most-missing columns (before cleaning)": []}))
display(baseline_top_missing)

# ============================
# Cleaning & Conversions
# ============================

# Standardize column names
df.columns = (df.columns.str.strip()
              .str.replace(r"\s+", "_", regex=True)
              .str.upper())

# Drop irrelevant columns
to_drop = ["ID","URL","ACTIVE_URLS","DUPLICATES","LAST_UPDATED_TIMESTAMP",
           "NAICS2","NAICS3","NAICS4","NAICS5","NAICS6","SOC_2","SOC_3","SOC_5"]
df.drop(columns=[c for c in to_drop if c in df.columns],
        inplace=True, errors="ignore")

# Convert dates
for col in [c for c in ["POSTED","UPDATED","DATE","JOB_POST_DATE"] if c in df.columns]:
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], errors="coerce")

# Convert salary columns
for col in ["SALARY","MINSALARY","MAXSALARY","ANNUAL_SALARY","HOURLY_RATE","PAY"]:
    if col in df.columns:
        df[col] = (df[col].astype(str)
                   .str.replace(r"[^0-9.\-]", "", regex=True)
                   .replace({"": np.nan, "-": np.nan})
                   .astype(float))

# Drop columns with >50% missing
df.dropna(axis=1, thresh=int(len(df)*0.5), inplace=True)

# Fill missing numeric values
num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()
if num_cols:
    if "INDUSTRY" in df.columns:
        df[num_cols] = df[num_cols].fillna(df.groupby("INDUSTRY")[num_cols].transform("median"))
    df[num_cols] = df[num_cols].fillna(df[num_cols].median())

# Fill missing categoricals with "Unknown"
for c in df.select_dtypes(include=["object"]).columns:
    df[c] = df[c].fillna("Unknown")

# Remove duplicates by key fields
dup_key = [c for c in ["TITLE","COMPANY","LOCATION","POSTED"] if c in df.columns]
if dup_key:
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=dup_key, keep="first")

# Snapshot after cleaning
rows_after, cols_after = df.shape
missing_cells_after = int(df.isna().sum().sum())
summary_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "metric": ["rows","columns","total missing cells"],
    "before": [rows_before, cols_before, missing_cells_before],
    "after":  [rows_after,  cols_after,  missing_cells_after]
})
after_top_missing = missing_summary(df).head(12)

# Show cleaned outputs
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 4: Cleaned dataset preview (first 5 rows)": []}))
display(df.head())
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 5: Dataset summary (before vs after cleaning)": []}))
display(summary_table)
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 6: Top 12 most-missing columns (after cleaning)": []}))

import re, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display

# Ensure dataset is loaded
try:
    df
except NameError:
    df = pd.read_csv("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv", low_memory=False)

# ============================
# Step 7: Remove Redundant Columns
# ============================

rows_before, cols_before = df.shape

explicit_drops = [
    "ID","URL","ACTIVE_URLS","DUPLICATES","LAST_UPDATED_TIMESTAMP",
    "TITLE_RAW","COMPANY_RAW","MODELED_EXPIRED","MODELED_DURATION",
    "NAICS2","NAICS2_NAME","NAICS3","NAICS3_NAME","NAICS4","NAICS4_NAME","NAICS5","NAICS5_NAME",
    "COUNTY_OUTGOING","COUNTY_NAME_OUTGOING","COUNTY_INCOMING","COUNTY_NAME_INCOMING",
    "MSA_OUTGOING","MSA_NAME_OUTGOING","MSA_INCOMING","MSA_NAME_INCOMING",
    "SOURCE_TYPES","SOURCES","TITLE_CLEAN"
]

flow_drop = [c for c in df.columns if re.search(r"(OUTGOING|INCOMING)$", c, flags=re.I)]

canon_keep = set()
for col in ["TITLE","COMPANY","LOCATION","POSTED","REMOTE_TYPE_NAME","EMPLOYMENT_TYPE_NAME",
            "NAICS6_NAME","CITY_NAME","COUNTY_NAME","MSA_NAME","STATE","STATE_NAME"]:
    if col in df.columns:
        canon_keep.add(col)

name_dupes = []
for base, alt in [("TITLE","TITLE_NAME"), ("COMPANY","COMPANY_NAME")]:
    if base in df.columns and alt in df.columns and alt not in canon_keep:
        name_dupes.append(alt)

to_drop = sorted(set([c for c in explicit_drops if c in df.columns] + flow_drop + name_dupes))
df.drop(columns=to_drop, inplace=True, errors="ignore")

rows_after_cols, cols_after_cols = df.shape

    "before": [rows_before, cols_before],

}))

# ============================
# Step 8: Remove Duplicates
# ============================

rows_before_dedup = len(df)
dedupe_key = [c for c in ["TITLE","COMPANY","LOCATION","POSTED"] if c in df.columns]
if not dedupe_key:
    dedupe_key = [c for c in ["TITLE","COMPANY","CITY_NAME","STATE","POSTED"] if c in df.columns]

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=dedupe_key, keep="first")

    "dedupe_key_used": [", ".join(dedupe_key) if dedupe_key else "(none)"],
    "rows_removed": [rows_before_dedup - rows_after_dedup],
    "rows_after": [rows_after_dedup]
}))

import re, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display

# ============================
# Step 9: Remove Extreme Values (Outliers) — Robust detection
# ============================

# Ensure salary-related columns are still in the dataset
df.columns = [c.strip().upper() for c in df.columns]

# Reload original salary info if needed
if not any(c in df.columns for c in ["SALARY","SALARY_FROM","SALARY_TO","ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD"]):
    try:
        df_raw = pd.read_csv("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv", low_memory=False)
        df_raw.columns = [c.strip().upper() for c in df_raw.columns]
        for c in ["SALARY","SALARY_FROM","SALARY_TO","ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD"]:
            if c in df_raw.columns and c not in df.columns:
                df[c] = df_raw[c]
    except Exception as e:
        display(pd.DataFrame({"⚠️ Warning": [f"Could not reload salary columns: {e}"]}))

# Detect any salary-related columns again
salary_cols = [c for c in df.columns if re.search(r"SALARY|PAY|WAGE", c, flags=re.I)]

if not salary_cols:
    display(pd.DataFrame({"⚠️ Warning": ["No salary-related columns found. Skipping Step 9."]}))
else:
    # 1️⃣ Coerce salary values to numeric
    for col in ["SALARY", "SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO"]:
        if col in df.columns:
            df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors="coerce")

    # 2️⃣ Compute midpoint
    if {"SALARY_FROM","SALARY_TO"}.issubset(df.columns):
        df["SALARY_MID"] = df[["SALARY_FROM","SALARY_TO"]].mean(axis=1)
    elif "SALARY" in df.columns:
        df["SALARY_MID"] = df["SALARY"]
    else:
        df["SALARY_MID"] = np.nan

    # 3️⃣ Convert to annual
    def to_annual(v, period):
        if pd.isna(v): 
            return np.nan
        p = str(period).lower() if pd.notna(period) else "year"
        factor = {"hour":2080, "day":260, "week":52, "month":12, "year":1}.get(p, 1)
        return float(v) * factor

    if "ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD" in df.columns:
        df["ANNUAL_SALARY"] = [to_annual(v, p) for v, p in zip(df["SALARY_MID"], df["ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD"])]
    else:
        df["ANNUAL_SALARY"] = df["SALARY_MID"]

    df.loc[df["ANNUAL_SALARY"] <= 0, "ANNUAL_SALARY"] = np.nan

    # 4️⃣ IQR outlier handling
    s = df["ANNUAL_SALARY"].dropna()
    low = high = np.nan
    removed_outliers = 0
    if len(s) > 0:
        q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
        iqr = q3 - q1
        low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
        mask = (df["ANNUAL_SALARY"] < low) | (df["ANNUAL_SALARY"] > high)
        removed_outliers = int(mask.sum())
        df.loc[mask, "ANNUAL_SALARY"] = np.nan

    # 5️⃣ Display summary
    display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 9: Salary Outlier Summary (IQR)": []}))
    display(pd.DataFrame({
        "salary_column_used": ["ANNUAL_SALARY"],
        "iqr_low_threshold": [low],
        "iqr_high_threshold": [high],
        "values_set_to_NaN": [removed_outliers],
        "remaining_with_salary": [int(df["ANNUAL_SALARY"].notna().sum())]
    }))


# ============================
# Step 10: Save Cleaned Dataset
# ============================

out_path = "Data/lightcast_clean_final.csv"
df.to_csv(out_path, index=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"📌 Step 10: Cleaned dataset saved": [out_path]}))

    s = (s.str.replace(r"\[|\]", "", regex=True)
          .str.replace('"', "", regex=False)
          .str.replace(r"\\n", " ", regex=True)
          .str.split(r"\s*,\s*|\|"))

    flat = s.explode().str.strip().replace("", np.nan).dropna()
    top_universe = flat.value_counts().head(50).index.tolist()

    # Symmetric pair counts
    counts = {}
    for skills in s:
        items = sorted(set([x.strip() for x in skills if x and x.strip() in top_universe]))
        for a, b in itertools.combinations(items, 2):
            counts[(a, b)] = counts.get((a, b), 0) + 1
            counts[(b, a)] = counts.get((b, a), 0) + 1

    def heatmap_top_n(n=15):
        topN = flat.value_counts().head(n).index.tolist()
        mat = pd.DataFrame(0, index=topN, columns=topN, dtype=int)
        for (a, b), v in counts.items():
            if a in topN and b in topN:
                mat.loc[a, b] += v
        np.fill_diagonal(mat.values, 0)
        return mat

    Ns = [10, 15, 20]
    frames = []
    for n in Ns:
        mat = heatmap_top_n(n)
        frames.append(go.Frame(
            name=f"Top {n}",
            data=[go.Heatmap(
                z=mat.values, x=mat.columns, y=mat.index,
                coloraxis="coloraxis",
                hovertemplate="Skill A: %{y}<br>Skill B: %{x}<br>Co-mentions: %{z}<extra></extra>"
            )]
        ))

    base = heatmap_top_n(10)
    fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Heatmap(
        z=base.values, x=base.columns, y=base.index,
        coloraxis="coloraxis",
        hovertemplate="Skill A: %{y}<br>Skill B: %{x}<br>Co-mentions: %{z}<extra></extra>"
    )])
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(text="Skill Co-occurrence Heatmap — choose Top-N", x=0.02),
        xaxis_title="Skill B", yaxis_title="Skill A",
        coloraxis=dict(colorscale="Purples"),
        margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10),
        updatemenus=[dict(
            type="buttons", x=1.0, xanchor="right", y=1.15, yanchor="top",
            buttons=[dict(label=f"Top {n}", method="animate",
                          args=[[f"Top {n}"], {"mode":"immediate","fromcurrent":True,
                                               "transition":{"duration":0},
                                               "frame":{"duration":0,"redraw":True}}]) for n in Ns]
        )]
    )
    fig.frames = frames
    fig.show()

    display(Markdown("**How to read:** Hotter cells = frequent pairs. Use those bundles for portfolio projects and resume bullets."))

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction
As of 2024, the global job market stands at a crucial crossroads, significantly shaped by the ongoing evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). This technology is transforming various sectors, including healthcare, finance, retail, and education. The shifts aren’t just about the types of jobs available; they’re also changing the way we work. Current studies reveal that while AI drives job displacement in routine and clerical roles, it simultaneously creates new opportunities that focus on technology, data, and human interaction (George ((2024)); Huang ((2024))). Tools like ChatGPT have added complexity, with predictions suggesting that over 30% of jobs could experience significant changes (Zarifhonarvar ((2024))). New roles, such as AI Solutions Architect and AI Bias Auditor, are emerging, highlighting the need for expertise in integrating AI into our workflows (George and George ((2025))). It’s clear that AI is not just about taking jobs away; it’s also sparking transformation, urging us to adapt, keep learning, and embrace innovation as we navigate the evolving career landscape.
As AI has gone from murmurs in the background to its sudden immediate dependencies for many many things in today’s age, questions, typically from fear, arise in the eye of the public. Will AI get rid of many jobs, crippling the job market? How is my job security in my current role going to change over the next couple of years? While AI brings humanity many benefits, it also has a very large grey area that could shift society in a negative direction if not managed properly. One thing that always pushes people forward in times of immense and sudden change, such as now, is to adapt. Rion ((2025)) states that “…there is a reduced risk of displacement occurring for high-skilled workers with AI encompassing elements of enhancement, whereas low-skilled workers are most at risk of displacement” (p. 2). The big hope with AI is that job displacement could potentially evolve into certain jobs and industries being repurposed for AI-centric functionalities. The change that AI has brought to the world and will continuously do, and in even bigger waves, is quickly making businesses adapt to the immediate benefits that it brings, but this is also a signal that individuals must pick up these skills to have a fighting chance in a job market that is turning into something entirely different.


Research Rationale
The increasing involvement of AI in various industries necessitates a deeper understanding of its impact on employment. Many conversations often frame AI as a threat to job security, but the reality is more nuanced. Research indicates that AI often triggers changes in work dynamics instead of leading to outright job loss. While there is no denial that some occupations in a number of sectors will be significantly altered if not replaced, as George ((2024)) points out, “AI is expected to result in more job movement than job elimination by boosting productivity, driving economic growth, altering job structures, and enabling sectors to transition” (p. 17). Recognizing these trends is crucial for both workers and policymakers as they work on strategies to ensure smooth transitions and equitable opportunities.
Additionally, the speed of this transformation is unlike anything we’ve seen before. Historical technological shifts unfolded over decades, while AI adoption is rapidly changing industries in just a few years. Today, workers find themselves in a labor market where traditional career paths exist alongside new, AI-driven opportunities. Zarifhonarvar ((2024)) emphasizes this urgency by stating, “32.8% of occupations could be fully impacted by ChatGPT, while 36.5% might experience a partial impact and 30.7% are likely to remain unaffected” (p. 100). This highlights the extensive and uneven impacts of AI disruption, emphasizing the need to examine its implications for job security, industry demand, and the emergence of new career fields. The function of this study is to assess the current state of the impact of AI on society, as of 2024, and try to get a better understanding of its pros and cons on the job market. According to Shen ((2024)), “AI technology is correlated with increasing the total number of jobs on the market. Thanks to more efficient labor productivity, capital deepening, and specialized division of labor from integrating digital technology, AI offsets the negative effects of robots on employment and significantly increases manufacturing enterprises’ market size and production scale, with a significant job creation effect” (p. 1). With the increased rate of integration of AI in most processes nowadays, there is actually a shift in the market and less of a depletion of jobs/job growth. Low-skilled workers have the biggest risk of being replaced by AI simply because the most mundane, repeatable jobs are the easiest for machines to replace. Developing certain skills relating to AI will prove very useful in this current job market because it is still such a fresh concept to the general population.


Literature Review
Recent research suggests that AI is more likely to lead to job shifting rather than large-scale, permanent job losses. While it’s true that some sectors may experience job displacement, George ((2024)) argues that the productivity gains associated with AI adoption consistently generate new employment opportunities. He explains that “displaced workers can transfer into new occupational jobs with adequate skilling and transition support rather than facing long periods of unemployment” (p. 17). This theme aligns with broader economic evidence showing that technological advancements typically create more jobs than they eliminate, even if the transition process can be rocky.
New job categories are emerging that didn’t exist just a decade ago. George and George ((2025)) highlight roles such as AI Solutions Architect and AI Bias Auditor, stating they are “not optional additions but essential components of sustainable AI strategy” (p. 58). Huang ((2024)) also notes that AI adoption is reshaping labor and capital in various industries, creating fresh opportunities while widening existing skill gaps. These trends underscore that AI isn’t merely automating routine tasks; it’s also driving innovation in job design, making continuous adaptation and skill development essential for today’s workforce.


Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with visualizations.
The Lightcast CSV file has a tremendous amount of data that would not make much sense to sort through manually. As a result, we have developed multiple tables that show a sample of the data from the Lightcast CSV. We show a sample of the first five rows which are raw and uncleaned. The second table is essentially a visualizer for the user showing how many rows, columns, and total missing cells there are in the file. The third table serves as a hub of information showing the percentage of data missing from the top 12 columns with the most missing data along with their types. The fourth table shows the data from the first table, but in a much cleaner fashion with all the relevant columns. The fifth tables is a comparative visual of how much data we were able to clean and filter throughout the entire process. As you can see, there are significantly less rows, columns, and total missing cells than before the cleanup. In the sixth and final table, all of the columns that had a certain percentage of missing data now have a missing data percentage of zero. This further shows that our process of cleaning up and filtering the data to pinpoint the exact information needed was successful.







References

George, Dr. A. S., and A. S. H. George. (2025): “The AI job revolution - how emerging roles are reshaping the future of work and creating new career pathways,” Zenodo, 3, 58–61.


Huang, X. (2024): “Dynamics of labor and capital in AI vs. Non-AI industries: A two-industry model analysis,” PLOS ONE, 19, 1–1.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, re
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# ---------- helpers that ALWAYS return Series ----------
def num_series(frame: pd.DataFrame, col: str):
    s = frame.get(col)
    if isinstance(s, pd.Series):
        return pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce")
    return pd.Series(np.nan, index=frame.index, dtype="float64")

def str_series(frame: pd.DataFrame, col: str, default=""):
    s = frame.get(col)
    if isinstance(s, pd.Series):
        return s.astype(str)
    return pd.Series(default, index=frame.index, dtype="object")

# ---------- FORCE LOAD: Lightcast dataset ----------
DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# unify column names
df.columns = [c.lower() for c in df.columns]

# ---------- LABEL CREATION (is_ai_role) ----------
if "is_ai_role" in df.columns:
    y_init = df["is_ai_role"]
else:
    text_cols = [c for c in [
        "title_raw","title","body",
        "skills_name","specialized_skills_name","software_skills_name","common_skills_name"
    ] if c in df.columns]
    if len(text_cols) == 0:
        y_init = pd.Series(0, index=df.index, dtype="int8")
    else:
        txt = df[text_cols].fillna("").astype(str).agg(" ".join, axis=1).str.lower()
        pattern = r"\b(ai|artificial intelligence|machine learning|ml|deep learning|data scientist|nlp|llm|transformer|pytorch|tensorflow|computer vision)\b"
        y_init = txt.str.contains(pattern, regex=True).astype("int8")

# ---------- FEATURES ----------
# Salary (annual-ish + outlier guard)
salary_main = num_series(df, "salary")
salary_from = num_series(df, "salary_from")
salary_to   = num_series(df, "salary_to")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)
salary      = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))

# Experience
exp_min     = num_series(df, "min_years_experience")
exp_max     = num_series(df, "max_years_experience")
experience  = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max).fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)
experience  = experience.mask(experience < 0)

# Remote
remote_text = str_series(df, "remote_type_name") if "remote_type_name" in df.columns else str_series(df, "remote")
remote      = remote_text.str.lower().isin(["remote","hybrid","remote/hybrid","remote - usa","remote - us"]).astype("int8")

# Region / State top-8
if "state_name" in df.columns:
    region_raw = str_series(df, "state_name")
elif "region" in df.columns:
    region_raw = str_series(df, "region")
else:
    region_raw = pd.Series("", index=df.index)

if region_raw.eq("").all():
    region_dum = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
else:
    top_regions = region_raw.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
    region_8 = region_raw.where(region_raw.isin(top_regions), "OTHER")
    region_dum = pd.get_dummies(region_8, prefix="region", dtype="int8")

# assemble
work = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        "salary": salary,
        "experience": experience,
        "remote": remote,
        "is_ai_role": y_init.astype("int8")
    }),
    region_dum
], axis=1)

# ---------- DIAGNOSTICS ----------
cls_counts = work["is_ai_role"].value_counts()
display(Markdown(
    f"- **Rows:** {len(work):,} • **AI roles:** {cls_counts.get(1,0):,} • **Non-AI:** {cls_counts.get(0,0):,}"
))

# ---------- DESCRIPTIVES ----------
if work["salary"].notna().sum() > 50:
    display(Markdown("### Salary Distribution — AI vs Non-AI"))
    px.box(
        work.dropna(subset=["salary"]),
        x="is_ai_role", y="salary", color="is_ai_role",
        labels={"is_ai_role":"Role (0=Non-AI, 1=AI)","salary":"Salary ($)"},
        title="Salary Comparison — AI vs Non-AI"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

display(Markdown("### Experience — AI vs Non-AI"))
px.box(
    work.dropna(subset=["experience"]),
    x="is_ai_role", y="experience", color="is_ai_role",
    labels={"is_ai_role":"Role (0=Non-AI, 1=AI)","experience":"Years"},
    title="Experience Comparison — AI vs Non-AI"
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

# ---------- CLASSIFICATION ----------
X = work[["salary","experience","remote"]].copy()
y = work["is_ai_role"].copy()

# If salary nearly all missing, drop it so rows don't collapse to 0
if X["salary"].notna().sum() < 50:
    X = X.drop(columns=["salary"])

mask_rows = y.isin([0,1]) & X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X.loc[mask_rows].fillna(0)
y = y.loc[mask_rows].astype(int)

cls_counts2 = y.value_counts()
display(Markdown(
    f"- **Classification rows:** {len(X):,} • **0:** {cls_counts2.get(0,0):,} • **1:** {cls_counts2.get(1,0):,}"
))

if len(X) < 100 or cls_counts2.min() == 0:
    display(Markdown("> ⚠️ Not enough balanced data to train classifiers (need both classes and ≥100 rows)."))
else:
    # stratify only if the smallest class will still have ≥2 rows in test split
    test_size = 0.25
    use_strat = (cls_counts2.min() * test_size) >= 2

    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=42, stratify=(y if use_strat else None)
    )

    scaler = StandardScaler()
    X_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
    X_test_s  = scaler.transform(X_test)

    # Logistic Regression
    logreg = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)
    logreg.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
    y_pred = logreg.predict(X_test_s)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred); f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred)
    display(Markdown(f"### Logistic Regression — Accuracy: **{acc:.3f}**, F1: **{f1:.3f}**"))
    px.imshow(
        confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=[0,1]),
        text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
        labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
        x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
        title="Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

    # Random Forest
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
    rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_test)
    acc_rf = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_rf); f1_rf = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_rf)
    display(Markdown(f"### Random Forest — Accuracy: **{acc_rf:.3f}**, F1: **{f1_rf:.3f}**"))
    px.imshow(
        confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_rf, labels=[0,1]),
        text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
        labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
        x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
        title="Confusion Matrix — Random Forest"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

    # Feature importances
    pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True).pipe(
        lambda s: px.bar(s, orientation="h",
            title="Random Forest Feature Importances (AI vs Non-AI)",
            labels={"value":"Importance","index":"Feature"})
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()
